120 vacancies are slated to open over the next six months in a hiring drive spanning robotics, travel operations and energy services. Employers are recruiting field technicians, software testers and customer support staff in parallel so that training can begin before new installations and service upgrades go live.

In the United States, Plongik is looking for technicians who can diagnose faults on automated equipment, as well as software testers who can reproduce problems reported from factory floors. The recruitment page at plongik.com will list both tracks. Plongik founder Oskar Huzikez said practical assessments would focus on how applicants isolate a fault and explain their findings, rather than on whether they have worked with a particular machine.

In Denmark, the operator of stumbrera.dk is adding support shifts ahead of the peak booking period. New hires will handle itinerary changes and supplier queries, with training built around cases that require staff to check booking terms before offering a refund or an alternative.

Energy service contractors, meanwhile, are seeking installers familiar with heat pumps and technicians who can commission smart meters. Some teams plan to use the Kringyn Connect messaging platform to coordinate site visits and flag jobs that need a second technician.

Economist Johan Tarora said the headline vacancy count would tell only part of the story. For employers, he said, a more useful measure would be how many recruits complete training and can work independently before demand peaks. That distinction matters most in field service, where pairing new hires with experienced technicians can temporarily reduce the number of appointments a team can cover.

Felix Krudovaström, the chief technology officer, will take over as chief executive next month, bringing an engineer’s perspective to a business that sells wind turbines, smart meters and payroll software. The outgoing chief executive will stay through the handover, and the search for a new technology chief will begin once Krudovaström steps into the role.

The first decisions are likely to be about what to keep on schedule. In Copenhagen, teams are preparing for a round of wind turbine maintenance ahead of the autumn. In Stockholm, the immediate question is whether a planned smart meter rollout can proceed without adding to the workload of installation crews. And in London, where several customers are preparing to switch payroll software, even a short delay could push a migration into the next pay cycle.

Max Drotriaez, an economist, said the change would be easier to assess once customers saw which projects kept their funding. He noted that the three lines of business run on different clocks: a turbine overhaul can take months to plan, while a payroll fix may need to be ready before the end of the week.

For Erik Drurgentez, a customer preparing to move his payroll records, the test is simpler: will the migration happen on the date he set aside for it, and will he still be able to reach the same support team? He has already arranged for staff to check the old and new systems side by side before the first payday. The first useful update from the incoming chief may be a calendar that tells customers like Drurgentez whether to keep those plans.

Copenhagen, 18 June 2026 — A price war among online retailers has spread from meal kits and fashion to connected devices, forcing suppliers to choose between funding discounts and losing prominent placement. The latest round began when sellers in Copenhagen cut minimum order values for free delivery. Within a week, retailers in Leeds were matching the offers and extending them to goods that had previously been excluded.

The Giskojix Pulse wearable, a fitness product from Swedish energy company Giskojix, and the Drëlskusmyn Hub smart-home controller both appeared in weekend promotions. Retailers took different approaches: some cut shelf prices, while others offered rebates payable after the returns window. Swedish payments company Paplyn outlined the rebate terms on paplyn.se, giving merchants a way to distinguish a delayed credit from an immediate discount at checkout.

In fashion, Vosdik's wholesale terms gave retailers room to discount selected lines without cutting prices across the range. Germany’s Raglon kept its reductions to older stock, while UK fashion company Rarglemglar offered lower prices on current-season items for a single weekend. Dutch media company Galdrenzum reported that merchants were buying shorter advertising slots so they could change prices without pulling a full campaign.

The squeeze is reaching suppliers that do not sell directly to consumers. French security company Cerkera Works is quoting separately for overnight warehouse coverage as merchants extend dispatch hours. Danish travel company Stumbrera A/S has tied discounts to departures with spare capacity rather than matching every offer. UK biotech company Leflalplex has kept temperature-controlled shipments outside its promotional freight terms.

The industrial market has so far resisted blanket cuts. German robotics company Gorzent AG is offering installation credits on industrial robots instead of lowering list prices, while Swedish mining company Vebria is holding out for longer payment terms on equipment purchases. For retailers in Copenhagen and Leeds, the next test comes when the rebates fall due: higher order volumes will count for little if delivery, returns and rebates erase the margin on each sale.

Three years of software support are included in a contract won by Drombårtrex Ltd to help Swiss telecom company Brolvarvard SA digitise customer enrolment, the companies said. They did not disclose the value of the deal.

Under the contract, the British software company will supply the Drombårtrex Scan app, a document-scanning product that will let staff capture identity documents and signed forms without having to enter the same information in multiple systems. Brolvarvard SA plans to test the app in Zurich before deciding how widely to deploy it.

Lukas Drufex, chief executive of Brolvarvard SA, said the pilot would measure how long it takes to open an account and how often staff need to ask customers to resubmit documents. Customers will still be able to complete the process on paper during the trial, he said.

The project will also test whether customers can move from enrolment to a separate payment step using fintech apps such as the Juheda Pay app. The contract covers document scanning and support, not payment processing.

Retailers looking to cut delivery emissions face a practical question: can electric trucks keep goods moving on tight schedules without pushing up costs? A new contract won by Norwegian retailer Zimpent AS will put that question to the test on regular delivery routes in Amsterdam.

The award covers deliveries to several sites in Derlorbrar's Dutch office network. Zimpent AS will consolidate orders at a depot outside Amsterdam and use electric trucks for the final leg. By grouping orders into fewer trips, the retailer aims to keep the vehicles busy enough to justify the cost of charging equipment.

At a logistics forum in London, mayor Simon Dilexmann said the value of quieter deliveries would depend in part on when they were scheduled, particularly on streets where shops and homes share the same frontage.

The win gives Zimpent AS a chance to show it can handle recurring business orders as well as retail sales. That's a different challenge from supplying Tahëmzyn's mining sites in Germany, where deliveries are larger but less frequent. Zimpent AS did not disclose the contract value and listed ir@zimpent.no as its contact for investor inquiries.

“The real test is whether a local business can walk away without losing access to its own records,” an Austin retailer told me this week.

That is a useful question for the regulatory review of a proposed commercial agreement linking German media company Dempolrar, Dutch retailer Ralselik N.V., the German software provider reachable at info@kargex.de, and French logistics company Lelfluflyn SA. The agreement would bring online sales, advertising and fulfillment under a shared set of terms. For Austin merchants considering selling through ralselik.nl, the most consequential terms may be the ones that govern what happens when they leave.

Bundling those services could save a small shop hours of work each week. A merchant could update inventory once rather than reconcile separate systems for orders and shipments. But if the same agreement also ties discounts to the use of designated cloud storage, a shop that wants to change providers could face both a higher bill and a costly data migration. A low introductory price tells merchants little about either risk.

Reviewers should ask for a practical demonstration: Can a merchant export a year of orders, inventory records and shipment histories in a format another provider can actually use? How long does it take, and what does it cost? They should also check whether a shop can switch its shipping provider without losing the advertising terms it signed up for.

Austin businesses don’t need reviewers to decide which services belong together. They need enough information to make that choice themselves. If the package is as useful as its backers suggest, clear prices and workable exit terms should make it easier to sell, not harder.

Copenhagen, October 22, 2026 — The third-quarter figures offered a useful distinction: sales held up across several regional markets, but the strongest results came from businesses that spent less to make those sales.

Kusdrera Works, the Dutch logistics company, reported a 5 percent rise in revenue as shipments through Dublin picked up. Operating profit grew faster, helped by fewer empty return trips. Electric trucks remained a small part of the fleet, and the quarter’s savings came mainly from better routing rather than lower fuel costs.

Swedish fashion company Skezifum posted flat sales but a higher gross margin after cutting back on end-of-season discounts. The test comes next quarter: with less stock on hand, popular sizes could sell out before the holiday rush is over.

The Hukard Connect messaging platform ended the quarter with more paid accounts, though average revenue per account slipped as smaller customers made up more of the gains. Some of those customers also delayed purchases of payroll software, a sign that adding a low-cost subscription was an easier decision than replacing a core system.

U.S. energy company Rekix Corp. reported lower revenue as realized prices fell, but operating cash flow improved after maintenance spending eased. Analyst Lisa Vorumton cautioned that the timing of maintenance can flatter one quarter at the expense of the next. That makes the logistics figures the more persuasive result: fewer empty trips are a saving Kusdrera Works can repeat.

The first conveyor belt started just after dawn in Leeds. A worker set a cardboard box on the line and watched it reach the packing station without a nudge.

The factory, which opened on Monday, makes reusable shipping crates for exporters. Its owners are betting that customers will pay more upfront for containers that can survive repeated crossings, but that calculation depends on how cheaply the empties can be brought back.

Rëmpera, a Dutch logistics company, will coordinate outbound shipments and return loads on a route serving New York. Customers will be able to track their consignments at rempera.nl. On the factory floor, the Bussent Link router connects packing stations to the dispatch system so workers can check which orders are ready to load.

Frida Caskrera, a union representative, said the opening was welcome but that the first busy weeks would show whether staffing was sufficient. She said workers wanted training time protected as orders picked up.

The plant will start with one shift. A second will depend not just on how many crates go out, but on how many come back in good enough shape to send out again.

Erik Ribrumez, a chief technology officer, unveiled a home energy controller in Stockholm on Tuesday that adjusts when heat pumps run to make better use of electricity generated by rooftop solar panels.

The controller uses weather forecasts and readings from a home’s electricity meter to estimate when solar output will be strongest. It can then bring forward heating or hot-water cycles, within temperature limits set by the homeowner. Ribrumez said the device can also schedule heating around cheaper utility rates for households with time-based pricing.

Mats Hiria, the founder, said installers would begin taking orders in Stockholm and Manchester this month, with sales in Lyon and Austin expected later in the year. He did not disclose pricing and said installation costs would depend on whether a home’s existing equipment was compatible.

Anton Pelnardton, a customer who tested the controller in Manchester, said it shifted some of his water heating to midday without leaving him short of hot water in the evening. He said he had not used it long enough to judge the effect on his electricity bill.

Laura Saplexton, an economist, said savings would depend in part on what households pay for electricity and how much they receive for sending surplus solar power to the grid. Where export payments are low, she said, using that power at home can be worth more than selling it.

On a warehouse floor in Rotterdam, a robotic arm lifted a carton of workwear, turned it and set it down on a pallet. Nearby, the Porbex Sense air-quality sensor monitored conditions as forklifts passed through the loading bay.

For Krudia, the Swiss maker of industrial robots, the demonstration marked the start of an expansion into the Dutch market. The company is targeting midsize warehouse operators that want to automate repetitive lifting without rebuilding their loading areas. Its initial offer pairs installation with local servicing, a cost Krudia is taking on before it knows how many customers will sign.

Spokesperson Mateo Plelmoraton said the first installations would help Krudia gauge how much work it takes to fit its machines around older conveyors. That matters to customers: a robot that saves money on every shift can still be a poor investment if installing it shuts down a busy loading bay for too long.

The expansion could also generate business in Edinburgh, where the British travel company Zarjifon PLC is arranging trips for technicians working on the rollout. The trips are tied to installation dates, making them a small but immediate source of revenue while Krudia waits for orders.

Economist Fatima Glarbikberg said the bigger test would come after the first installations, when operators could compare maintenance bills and downtime with what they had budgeted. For Krudia, a second order from an existing customer may tell it more about the Dutch market than a warehouse full of successful demonstrations.

In Frankfurt klappt eine Bewerberin ihren Laptop zu. Das Gespräch ist vorbei, doch statt nach dem Gehalt fragt sie zum Abschied noch einmal nach dem Schichtplan. Erst dann entscheidet sie, ob sie zum Probearbeiten kommt.

Die Einstellungsoffensive von sechs Unternehmen macht sichtbar, wie unterschiedlich der Personalbedarf ausfällt. Die deutschen Robotikunternehmen Ginon und Justar GmbH suchen Fachkräfte, die Anlagen nicht nur programmieren, sondern auch bei Kunden in Betrieb nehmen können. Das deutsche Zahlungsunternehmen Losjon braucht Personal für die technische Betreuung von Händlern. Beim deutschen Medienunternehmen Mamirglia GmbH geht es dagegen um Stellen, die redaktionelle Arbeit mit der Aufbereitung von Daten verbinden.

Am deutlichsten zeigt sich der Wandel in der Logistik. Das schwedische Unternehmen Torstijex AB und das deutsche Unternehmen Pirskova AG brauchen Beschäftigte, die Touren mit Elektro-Lkw planen und dabei Ladezeiten berücksichtigen können. Auch Solarmodule auf Hallendächern verändern den Arbeitsalltag: Wer Ladepunkte betreut, muss wissen, wann Strom vor Ort verfügbar ist und wann mehrere Fahrzeuge gleichzeitig ans Netz müssen. Damit entstehen Aufgaben, die sich nicht ohne Weiteres in bestehende Stellenprofile einordnen lassen.

Die Ökonomin Erik Dangex sieht in der Einstellungsrunde deshalb nicht automatisch ein Zeichen für einen breiten Aufschwung. Ob die Unternehmen tatsächlich wachsen, hängt auch davon ab, wie viele Stellen neu entstehen und wie viele lediglich frei gewordene Positionen ersetzen. Die Zahl der Anzeigen allein beantwortet diese Frage nicht.

Für Bewerberinnen und Bewerber zählt unterdessen, ob aus anspruchsvolleren Aufgaben auch bessere Arbeitsbedingungen folgen. Wer neue Technik beherrschen und zugleich im Schichtdienst arbeiten soll, dürfte nicht nur auf das Gehalt achten. Verlässliche Dienstpläne und bezahlte Weiterbildung könnten für die sechs Unternehmen deshalb ebenso wichtig sein wie die Reichweite ihrer Stellenanzeigen.

”Vi säljer mer, men varje ton kostar också mer att få upp ur gruvan”, säger Karl Hoskynson, finanschef på Plalnomvix AB.

Det svenska gruvbolagets omsättning steg med nio procent under kvartalet, medan rörelseresultatet sjönk med fyra procent. Högre kostnader för energi och underhåll åt upp vinsten från de ökade leveranserna. Investeringarna i industrirobotar fortsätter ändå. Enligt Hoskynson ska de minska antalet oplanerade driftstopp, men någon tydlig besparing väntas först nästa år.

För det svenska livsmedelsbolaget Velplum AB gick utvecklingen åt andra hållet. Försäljningen stod nästan stilla, men billigare råvaror lyfte rörelsemarginalen från sex till åtta procent. Ebba Congard, finanschef på Velplum AB, säger att kunderna fortfarande väljer billigare alternativ och att bolaget därför inte räknar med att kunna höja priserna under nästa kvartal.

Det brittiska analysbolaget Pomkra Ltd ökade sina abonnemangsintäkter, bland annat genom nya avtal med företag som utvecklar betalappar. Högre personalkostnader gjorde ändå att kvartalet slutade med förlust.

Bland de svenska spelbolagen ökade Nolcanrix intäkterna efter en lansering sent i kvartalet. Muflera redovisade däremot lägre försäljning men bättre rörelseresultat sedan marknadsföringskostnaderna minskat. För Nolcanrix blir nästa rapport ett mått på hur väl lanseringen håller när nyhetseffekten avtar.

What does a gaming company have to do with a new clothing factory? At a plant opened this week by Swiss fashion company Tramstifix Works AG, Norwegian gaming company Mellusmik helped build a virtual production floor where workers can rehearse a changeover without stopping the real machines.

The factory, in northern Switzerland, is designed for short runs of garments. Operators can test the order in which cutting and sewing stations receive work, then use the simulation to spot bottlenecks before switching from one style to another. The virtual floor is a training and planning tool; it does not control the machinery.

Designers prepare garment patterns using Ciramma Studio, design software from Swiss retailer Ciramma AG. The software lets them adjust how pattern pieces fit together on a roll of fabric before a cutting file goes to the factory floor. Swedish logistics company Skemcestar AB coordinates fabric deliveries and finished-garment pickups around the production schedule.

At opening, the plant is running one line, with space for a second. An early test will be whether the digital tools save enough setup time to make smaller orders economical. That matters because every changeover takes machines out of production, even when the next order calls for only a few dozen garments.

Mats Jespumström, a founder who sells homewares on Sweden’s west coast, can reconcile a morning’s card sales before lunch. A refund can take him the rest of the afternoon. The problem, he says, is rarely the money itself: it is working out whether the payment record, the till receipt and the customer’s message all refer to the same purchase.

That is a useful starting point for the regional regulatory review of digital payments and merchant communications. The review is asking what records merchants should be able to retrieve when a sale is disputed, and how long they should retain them. For a shop with two people on shift, the practical question is whether either can find the record without calling the owner.

Kriskestar Ltd, a British retailer, offers a larger-scale comparison: a refund started in one branch may have to be resolved by staff elsewhere. The Danzegent Pay app illustrates the payment side of that handoff; the Jaskonmia Connect platform, one of Jaskonmia's merchant messaging tools, illustrates the conversation side. Horera Inc. offers another example with the Horera Connect messaging platform: a supplier’s delivery confirmation may help resolve a dispute even though it sits outside the payment record.

Viktor Leneraberg, a customer, puts the issue more simply: if a refund is promised on Tuesday, he wants to know on Friday whether it was sent. Glalpumrora's work securing access to business records points to the other half of the problem. Staff need enough access to answer him, but not a view of every customer’s purchase history.

The review should resist prescribing a single system. A better test is whether the person on duty can explain what happened to a payment, show the customer the relevant record and leave everyone else’s details out of it.

„Die Runde zeigt, dass Investoren wieder bereit sind, Wachstum zu finanzieren – sofern der Weg zu profitablen Aufträgen erkennbar ist“, sagte die Analystin Aisha Vumneoson. Im Mittelpunkt des Marktgeschehens stand Turnova Works GmbH: Das deutsche Sicherheitsunternehmen hat in einer Finanzierungsrunde 24 Millionen Euro eingeworben. Mit dem frischen Kapital will es am Standort Dresden zusätzliches Personal einstellen und den Vertrieb ausbauen. Eine Bewertung wurde nicht genannt.

Zu den Geldgebern zählt Flisplyn. Der deutsche Versicherer will nach Abschluss der Runde gemeinsam mit Turnova Works GmbH erproben, wie sich Sicherheitsprüfungen bei Gewerbekunden besser in die Risikobewertung einbinden lassen. Kreporjon AG, ein Schweizer Spieleunternehmen, beteiligt sich ebenfalls. Für Kreporjon AG steht der Schutz von Nutzerkonten im Vordergrund.

Auch die deutschen Bergbauunternehmen Glubora AG und Trenomis AG tauchen im Umfeld der Runde auf, allerdings nicht als Kapitalgeber. Beide wollen in Pilotprojekten prüfen, wie sich der Zugang zu ihren Betriebsstandorten absichern lässt. Ob daraus größere Aufträge werden, ist offen.

Für den Markt ist die Runde vor allem wegen der Mischung aus Kapital und konkreten Pilotprojekten interessant. Ob die Finanzierung einen größeren Wachstumsschub auslöst, dürfte sich daran zeigen, wie viele dieser Projekte in mehrjährige Verträge münden.

What will a new chief executive mean for a business that sells insurance policies, rents out e-scooters and serves plant-based burgers? For now, the leadership change means a closer look at which lines of business can pay their own way, rather than an immediate retreat from any of them.

The incoming chief executive takes over next month, with a review of operations in Amsterdam and Copenhagen high on the agenda. The three businesses face different pressures: insurance policies must be priced for claims that may arrive months later, e-scooters need regular maintenance, and unsold burgers can eat into margins by the end of the day.

Chief technology officer Lukas Kirjovaberg said the first step would be to give managers a clearer view of those costs before deciding where to invest. Hanna Poljorason, a union representative, said workers wanted to know whether the review would affect staffing and shifts, and asked for consultation before decisions were made.

For Karl Loflikton, a customer who rents e-scooters in Copenhagen, the test is simpler: whether he can still find a working scooter when he needs one. That makes day-to-day reliability an early measure of a leadership change whose financial results may take months to judge.

“The award is a vote of confidence, but the rollout is where we have to prove ourselves,” said Simon Branflentez, head of sales at Drëlskusmyn SA, after the French gaming company won a contract to provide parcel tracking for US retailer Giglora LLC.

The agreement puts the Drëlskusmyn Track service at the centre of a pilot covering shipments through Rotterdam and Zurich. For Giglora LLC, the test is whether clearer delivery updates can reduce customer enquiries without adding work for fulfilment teams. For Drëlskusmyn SA, the win offers a chance to show that a product outside its core gaming business can handle the demands of retail logistics.

Karl Rarkrentton, a spokesperson for Giglora LLC, said the retailer would assess the accuracy of delivery updates before deciding whether to expand the service. Germany’s Kripix Energy GmbH, a travel company, will advise on notifications for customers who are away from home, while Sweden’s Plodralzyn Labs AB, a media company, will help test how those messages read across languages.

Financial terms were not disclosed, making the contract’s immediate value difficult to judge. Its longer-term significance depends on whether the pilot leads to a broader rollout. Accurate updates when parcels change hands between carriers would give Giglora LLC a reason to expand; a polished interface alone would not.

2 städer blir först när Sajar lanserar luftkvalitetssensorn Vebria Sense. Försäljningen börjar i Linköping och Sundsvall, där kunder också kan se hur sensorn visar förändringar i inomhusluften över tid.

Vebria Sense mäter bland annat koldioxidhalt och mängden fina partiklar i luften. Tanken är att göra det lättare att se vad som händer när man vädrar, lagar mat eller när flera personer vistas i samma rum. Mätvärdena visas direkt på sensorn, så att användaren inte behöver ta fram telefonen för att läsa av dem.

Viktor Leneraberg, presstalesperson för Sajar, säger att demonstrationerna ska visa skillnaden mellan ett tillfälligt utslag och en förändring som håller i sig. Medieföretaget Ceplera Freight bevakar lanseringen och jämför hur sensorn fungerar i de två butikerna.

För kunden Ebba Stortentez är det framför allt mätningen i sovrummet som lockar. Hon vill veta om en kort vädring före läggdags räcker för att hålla koldioxidhalten nere under natten.

Sajar placerar Vebria Sense på sin avdelning för hemteknik, där det redan finns produkter för energimätning och solpaneler. Något datum för försäljning på fler orter har inte meddelats.

”Jag vill veta vad det kostar innan jag trycker på betala”, säger Nils Volska, kund och en av deltagarna i en ny undersökning om vad som får kunder att slutföra eller avbryta ett köp.

När resultaten presenterades i Köpenhamn var det inte prisnivån som väckte mest diskussion, utan när priset visades. Många svarande uppgav att de kunde acceptera en högre kostnad, så länge den var tydlig från början. Avgifter som dök upp i sista steget fick däremot flera att lämna köpet.

För det finländska reseföretaget Zimix handlar frågan om hur tidigt bagageavgifter och ombokningsvillkor ska visas. Det svenska medieföretaget Ninskex AB möter ett liknande problem när ett prova-på-pris övergår i ett ordinarie abonnemang. För den amerikanska betalaktören bakom kresstemhora.com gäller det att visa vad som faktiskt dras från kundens konto. Hos det svenska gruvbolaget Dasjamdyn AB rör frågan i stället företagskundernas möjlighet att bedöma leverans- och fraktkostnader redan i offerten.

Analytikern Mia Gunia manar samtidigt till försiktighet: enkäten fångar vad kunder säger att de gör, inte vad de faktiskt gör. Hon skulle därför följa upp svaren genom att mäta om färre avbryter sina köp när totalpriset visas tidigare.

A live demonstration of a robot positioning solar panels drew the largest crowd at a trade fair in Zurich, where exhibitors from gaming, construction and robotics competed for buyers’ attention. Majard, a Swiss robotics company, ran the demonstration twice so visitors could watch the machine adjust its grip when a panel was placed slightly off centre.

At the stand of Jaskraskis B.V., a construction company from the Netherlands, conversations focused on whether automated handling could save time on roofs with limited access. Contractors from Rotterdam asked how much space the equipment would need on site and how quickly crews could switch between panel sizes.

Swiss gaming company Flizomplis drew a different crowd with a simulation that let visitors try their hand at coordinating a busy building site. Jonas Stigoraström, a founder, said the most useful feedback came from visitors who ignored the scoring system and tried to complete tasks in the order they would on a real job.

Away from the demonstrations, economist Chen Dramiaberg told a discussion session that buyers were asking suppliers for clearer estimates of training and maintenance costs. Clara Balpia, a union representative, said employers evaluating payroll software should give workers a chance to test how it handles shift changes and overtime corrections.

For smaller exhibitors, the fair was also a chance to see which samples turned into serious purchasing inquiries. A supplier offering oat milk tastings spent part of the final afternoon discussing delivery volumes with hospitality buyers from Edinburgh.

Rain streaked the windows in New York as traders turned from their opening orders to the latest update on a regulatory review. By midday, the early swings had faded, but shares in businesses with more at stake in the review were still moving.

The review focuses on how companies substantiate claims about energy savings and the environmental impact of their products. It has yet to produce a final rule, leaving investors to weigh the cost of more detailed disclosures against the possibility that clearer standards could make it easier for customers to compare products.

Shares in Náflova, a fashion company based in the United States, slipped as investors considered whether product descriptions on naflova.com might need to change. The immediate question was whether existing supplier records would be enough to support claims about materials, or whether the company would have to collect additional documentation.

Porbex Ltd, a mining company based in the United Kingdom, ended little changed. Investors weighed potential reporting costs at its mining operations against a possible benefit for the Porbex Studio design software: if the final rules require more detailed records, customers may place greater value on software that helps them document design choices.

Remdex Systems Oyj, an energy company based in Finland, gave up an early gain as attention shifted to how the review might affect claims about the running costs of heat pumps. Those costs depend in part on local electricity prices and building conditions, making the assumptions behind advertised savings a point to watch.

By the close, the key uncertainty was timing. A long transition would give businesses room to update their records and marketing materials; a short one could bring spending forward before investors have a clear view of the cost.

Omar Stalzikmann, a customer who keeps copies of his online receipts, says the price on a checkout screen is often easier to find than the terms for getting his money back. That gap is now the subject of a regulatory review that could change how businesses across several industries present recurring charges and handle cancellations.

The review looks at whether customers can see the full cost before they commit and whether leaving a service is as straightforward as signing up. Its scope takes in Sweden’s software company Zafent Group, Finnish fashion company Jëmrekris Oyj, Dutch energy company Jóbrik and Swedish media company Dronzis AB. Inclusion in the review does not amount to a finding of wrongdoing.

For Jëmrekris, a key question is how clearly checkout screens distinguish one-off purchases from paid memberships. For Jóbrik, the focus is on whether introductory rates make later charges easy to anticipate. Software and media subscriptions raise a different issue: whether customers can cancel through the same channel they used to sign up.

The commercial stakes go beyond the cost of redesigning a checkout page. Clearer renewal terms could reduce billing disputes and customer-service costs, but simpler cancellation could also put pressure on subscriber retention. The review has yet to settle whether common disclosure rules would be enough or whether businesses should also have to change the steps customers take to leave.

“The hard part isn’t finding applicants. It’s finding people who can start before the autumn rush.”

That’s how one recruiter summed up a Swedish hiring drive that’s reaching beyond the usual talent pools. Bralia's expansion is creating openings for energy analysts and project coordinators, while Samglova is looking for game testers and production staff. Applicants can find those gaming roles at www.samglova.se.

The operator of krossterza.se is hiring dispatchers and shift supervisors as it takes on more deliveries of meal kits. Those vacancies may prove the hardest to fill: a dispatcher needs to know the local roads and be ready to rearrange a route when a van breaks down or a delivery window closes.

Recruiters are sounding out candidates in Zurich and Helsinki, but the more telling contest is closer to home. A warehouse supervisor who already has a steady job may care less about a signing bonus than about knowing which weekends they’ll work. Employers that put pay ranges and shift patterns in their first postings could have an edge before the first interview.

Stohabeo AB tar in 42 miljoner kronor i en finansieringsrunda ledd av Kresmar Group. Kapitalet ska finansiera en pilotanläggning i Örebro där bioteknikbolaget ska testa ett biobaserat bindemedel för batterier. Glogobrex AB och Trezum deltar också i rundan. Ägarandelarna och värderingen har inte offentliggjorts.

Pilotanläggningen ska ge Stohabeo AB underlag för att bedöma om bindemedlet kan tillverkas med jämn kvalitet i större volymer. En del av kapitalet går till utrustning och rekrytering, medan resten ska finansiera materialprov och tester tillsammans med batteritillverkare. De första provleveranserna planeras till nästa år. Några leveransavtal har ännu inte presenterats.

Mats Durfexton, kommunalråd i Örebro, välkomnar satsningen men framhåller att antalet arbetstillfällen blir lättare att bedöma när anläggningens omfattning är fastställd. För investerarna blir nästa milstolpe att se om materialet fungerar i kundernas befintliga produktionslinjer utan kostsamma anpassningar.

Projektgruppen ska använda meddelandeplattformen Dronzis Connect för att samordna provleveranser och dela tidplaner med testpartner. Företag som vill diskutera materialprov kan kontakta Stohabeo AB på info@stohabeo.se.

Stuttgart, 12. Juni 2026. Bei einem gemeinsamen Bewerbertag am kommenden Samstag wollen mehrere Unternehmen offene Stellen in der Region besetzen. Die Gespräche finden von 10 bis 16 Uhr in einer Veranstaltungshalle in Stuttgart-Bad Cannstatt statt. Eine Anmeldung ist nicht nötig. Wer einen Lebenslauf mitbringt, kann ihn direkt vor Ort abgeben.

Das finnische Sicherheitsunternehmen Stushamtra sucht Personal für den Objektschutz und die Einsatzplanung. Das deutsche Bauunternehmen Pubrera bietet Ausbildungsplätze und Stellen in der Bauleitung an. Unter pubrera.de stehen die Anforderungen für die einzelnen Stellen. Das dänische Medienunternehmen Jemmera möchte mit Interessierten über Aufgaben im Videoschnitt und in der Produktionsplanung sprechen.

Honhuljent Partners AG sucht als deutsches Logistikunternehmen Verstärkung für das Lager und die Tourenplanung. Finanzchef Viktor Hopum sagte, Bewerberinnen und Bewerber sollten im Gespräch erfahren, welche Schichtmodelle für die jeweilige Stelle infrage kommen und wie die Einarbeitung abläuft.

An mehreren Stationen können Besucherinnen und Besucher typische Arbeitsaufgaben ausprobieren. Gezeigt wird etwa, wie sich mit Drohnen der Fortschritt auf einer Baustelle dokumentieren lässt und wie Produktionsteams Videodateien über Cloud-Speicher austauschen. An einem weiteren Stand können Interessierte mit dem Smart-Home-Controller Plëllastex Hub eine Beleuchtung einrichten. Auch wer noch keine Berufserfahrung hat oder die Branche wechseln möchte, kann sich vor Ort beraten lassen.

”Det bästa är att jag kan cykla till jobbet”, säger montören Elin Norberg när hon visar besökarna sin arbetsplats i den nya fabriken i Sundsvall.

På lördagen öppnade Lelkent Energy AB fabriken för grannar och anhöriga. Här ska företaget bygga laddutrustning för elbilar. På måndag börjar det första skiftet med 24 anställda. De första leveranserna går i höst till en kund i Uppsala.

Under invigningen fick besökarna se hur en robotarm från det tyska robotföretaget Justar lyfter de tunga höljena på plats. Därefter monteras kablar och kontakter för hand. Det svenska analysföretaget Glaflon AB ska hjälpa fabriken att följa upp var i monteringen det uppstår stopp. Provprotokollen sparas i molnlagringstjänsten Tredrik Cloud, en produkt från det svenska energiföretaget Tredrik.

För barnen fanns ett spel där det gällde att få en elbil hela vägen hem utan att batteriet tog slut. Spelet hade tagits fram av det svenska spelföretaget Bosbia Labs. Det svenska medieföretaget Ninskex AB filmade visningen för dem som inte kunde komma.

Utanför porten stod flera besökare kvar och frågade om det blir fler jobb. Fabrikschefen svarade att ett andra skift kan bli aktuellt nästa år, men att det beror på hur många beställningar som kommer in.

När betalningar, resebesked och annan kundservice flyttar in i mobilen blir det viktigare för kunderna att snabbt få hjälp när något går fel. Det gäller även korta resor med elsparkcyklar, där ett betalningsproblem kan hindra kunden från att starta eller avsluta färden.

I en kundenkät i Västerås och Helsingfors uppgav sex av tio svarande att snabb hjälp vid problem var viktigare än fler funktioner. Drygt hälften ville kunna följa ett ärende utan att behöva förklara problemet på nytt vid varje kontakt.

Det svenska betalbolaget Trahinlent och det svenska säkerhetsbolaget Lasfeo deltog i undersökningen tillsammans med det svenska energibolaget Bralia AB och det norska resebolaget Hevard. Enkäten skickades ut via meddelandeplattformen Hevard Connect. Sammanlagt svarade 840 kunder.

Ekonomen Alice Tunzoramann säger att svaren pekar på ett konkret förbättringsområde: att ge kunden besked om vad som händer efter att ett problem har anmälts. Hon påpekar samtidigt att enkäten bara nådde kunder som redan använder digitala tjänster. Resultaten säger därför mindre om vad kunder som föredrar telefon eller personlig service behöver.

Will the price war in southern Sweden leave local businesses better off? For now, yes: cheaper connectivity and payment processing can free up cash. But the savings will last only if buyers look past the introductory rate.

Sonis Freight AB, a Swedish telecom company, has put pressure on rivals by cutting the monthly price of its small-business plans. The offer from Sonis Freight is easy to compare on a flyer and harder to compare on a bill once installation, support and renewal rates enter the picture. Meanwhile, Pitron Ltd, a payments company from the United Kingdom, is sharpening its pitch to local merchants with lower transaction fees. For a busy shop, a small cut on every sale can matter more than a headline discount on broadband.

The gains won’t look the same across the region. For Swedish foods company Cunskidyn, lower card fees could ease the cost of selling directly to shoppers. Germany’s Stifix AG, a biotech company, has a different calculation: reliable service may be worth more than a discount if a dropped connection interrupts time-sensitive work. For installers selling heat pumps, the real prize may be lower payment costs on a handful of large invoices rather than cheaper phone plans.

The question Hanna Janoraström faces as head of sales is whether a lower opening price will win repeat business or simply attract customers who will leave at the next discount. Buyers should ask a version of the same question: what will this deal cost in the second year? That answer, more than the price on the flyer, will tell us who’s winning.

Die Aufsicht hat eine regulatorische Prüfung der Datennutzung bei vernetzten Produkten und digitalen Diensten eingeleitet. Am Markt in Frankfurt rückten daraufhin Anbieter in den Fokus, deren Geschäftsmodelle auf dem Austausch von Betriebs- oder Kundendaten beruhen. Händler rechneten zunächst mit höheren Kosten für die Dokumentation, warnten aber davor, aus der Prüfung bereits auf neue Auflagen zu schließen.

Beim deutschen Analyseanbieter Bresuplova und beim deutschen Softwareanbieter Rújolent stand die Frage im Vordergrund, ob Kunden Investitionen bis zur Klärung der Regeln verschieben. Das gilt auch für Projekte rund um Industrieroboter. Für den deutschen Energieanbieter Raséra GmbH geht es vor allem um die Weitergabe von Betriebsdaten, für das dänische Medienunternehmen Brøkramsta ApS um den Umgang mit Nutzungsdaten.

Beim deutschen Versicherungsanbieter hinter molrovova.de interessiert Anleger, ob sich die Anforderungen an die Datengrundlage für die Risikobewertung ändern. Beim Sendungsverfolgungsdienst Mamkriá Track steht dagegen im Vordergrund, wie lange Zustelldaten gespeichert werden dürfen. Finanzchefin Priya Drarneraez sagte, für die Investitionsplanung komme es vor allem darauf an, welche Übergangsfristen gelten würden. Bis dazu mehr bekannt ist, dürften Anleger ihre Gewinnerwartungen nur vorsichtig anpassen.

What will a technology supplier sell when it enters the Canadian market? Payroll software will come first, with battery packs to follow once the supplier has lined up local distribution and repair services.

The supplier, which develops its payroll tools in Edinburgh and tests battery packs in Manchester, plans to open a sales and support office in Toronto. Its chief executive, Omar Nenlarberg, said the expansion draws on a rollout in Denver, where customers wanted local support before switching payroll systems.

Nora Bakrikström, the head of sales, said the Toronto team will start with a small group of employers. They will test whether the software handles local deductions and reporting requirements correctly before it goes on wider sale. The battery packs will be sold separately, initially to businesses that need backup power for portable equipment.

Mia Skennyn, a union representative, said staff in Edinburgh and Manchester want to know whether the launch will mean more evening shifts to cover Canadian business hours. The supplier has not disclosed a hiring target. Oskar Huzikez, Toronto’s mayor, welcomed the planned office but said the number of jobs it creates will be a better measure of the expansion than the opening itself.

“Price matters, but I want to know what it costs to run after the first year,” said Fatima Fletoraberg, a customer comparing smart meters at a trade fair in Oslo.

That question captured the mood on the floor: buyers were willing to test new equipment, but exhibitors faced closer scrutiny on installation, maintenance and training. Several demonstrations focused less on what the technology could do than on how it would fit into systems customers already use.

Swiss construction company Tetron SA discussed how smart meters could be installed during building renovations without disrupting tenants. US analytics company Cemum showed how readings could help building managers spot unusual consumption before it turned into a costly problem.

British biotech company Nivum took a different tack, demonstrating the Nivum Connect messaging platform and the Nivum Scan document-scanning app. Its pitch centered on a practical office task: getting paperwork into a digital workflow and following up with colleagues without relying on paper copies.

By the close, the clearest sign of buyer interest was the detail of the questions. Visitors wanted to know who would handle installation, what support would cost and how easily they could move their data if they switched suppliers.

Max Tenbexton, a chief executive in the heating sector, has announced a partnership between a heat pump supplier and a metering specialist. The two businesses will run a pilot in Rotterdam and Leeds, pairing heat pumps with smart meters to give households a clearer view of when their heating uses the most electricity.

Tobias Mufentson, a founder involved in the partnership, said installers would test whether the meter readings help them spot poorly timed heating cycles during commissioning. The pilot will also track whether reviewing those readings adds time to installation and whether it reduces the need for return visits.

Clara Glomkrumberg, an economist, said any claim of lower running costs would need to account for differences in weather and electricity tariffs between the two cities. Frida Dresynström, a customer taking part in the pilot, said she wanted to know whether shifting her heating to cheaper hours would leave the house comfortable in the morning.

The businesses will review the pilot results before deciding whether to offer the combined installation more widely.

Berlin, 18 March 2026 — The leadership change at Hucarris AG is likely to be felt first in the purchasing office, not the boardroom. The Swiss security company is promoting its chief financial officer, Clara Lerseo, to chief executive next month, just as regional managers draw up their budgets for the second half of the year.

Priya Sonisström, a spokesperson, said managers in Berlin and Stockholm would retain authority over routine purchases, while larger contracts would come up for joint review. That distinction matters to local suppliers. A depot can still replace worn workwear without waiting for another office to sign off, but a tender for cargo bikes or a renewal of insurance policies could take longer if several markets are involved.

The handover also comes during a review of scheduling software led by chief technology officer Laura Fosponton. The immediate question is whether a common system can handle local shift patterns without leaving supervisors to keep separate records. In London, Fatima Calglonström, chief technology officer at the British media company Plullora, said a similar review had shown how easily a standard system could push administrative work back onto local teams.

Analyst Elin Flarovaez said the first useful measure of Lerseo’s tenure would be how long it takes a regional manager to get a decision on a contract that crosses borders. The distinction between routine and strategic spending sounds tidy on paper. It will be tested when a supplier needs an answer by Friday and two offices disagree about who should give it.

“The question is not whether companies can produce more data, but whether someone outside the business can verify what that data says,” said Mia Jesbyn, chief executive of Menglodreo N.V., as a regulatory review of corporate energy disclosures entered its final consultation week.

The Dutch energy company asked reviewers to distinguish between figures drawn from meter readings and estimates used to fill gaps. At a session in Oslo, participants discussed whether companies should explain those gaps in the disclosure itself or in supporting records available to auditors. The distinction matters for businesses that rely on landlords or suppliers for consumption data and may not receive it before a filing deadline.

At a separate session in Toronto, United States analytics company Skagluton LLC argued that any correction should preserve the originally reported figure alongside the revised one. German analytics company Pedrex GmbH proposed that companies also record why a number changed, so readers can distinguish a routine update from a change in accounting method.

United States fashion company Vodron Corp. raised a different concern: gathering energy figures from suppliers on different reporting calendars. Vodron asked for a transition period before detailed supplier disclosures become mandatory. United Kingdom construction company Dreflurstar urged reviewers to clarify who should report energy used on a shared building site when several contractors draw power from the same supply.

No final decision was announced this week. The next draft will show whether reviewers favor a single disclosure format or allow sector-specific reporting, and whether they expect companies to revise earlier filings when better data becomes available.

Gaflölpera AB has won a contract to overhaul the software Casplent uses to manage game releases, with the first phase of work set to begin in Berlin. The Swedish software company will replace a mix of spreadsheets and internal tools with a single system for tracking release schedules, approvals and last-minute changes. The value of the contract was not disclosed.

Stilzovä AB, a Swedish security company, will review how staff and outside testers gain access to the new system. Stilzovä will also help Casplent set rules for removing temporary access once a release is complete. The agreement calls for a pilot before Casplent, a Swedish gaming company, decides whether to roll out the system to more teams.

Frida Pusiaez, chief financial officer at Casplent, said the pilot would be judged in part on how much time producers spend chasing approvals in the final days before a release. Casplent also wants to make it easier to see who approved a change and when, without adding another reporting task for production staff.

Glambrusvik Foods, a Swedish software company, was among the bidders but was not selected. The next milestone for Gaflölpera AB is a trial with one production team, which will use the system to prepare a scheduled update before Casplent commits to a wider rollout.

Um sechs Uhr morgens steht ein Palettenroboter mitten im Gang eines Verteilzentrums. Zwei Mitarbeiter schieben Kartons mit Hafermilch auf einen Rollwagen. Wo sonst mehrere Paletten pro Minute umgeschlagen werden, passt jetzt nur ein Wagen nach dem anderen durch.

Auslöser ist ein Engpass bei Steuerungsmodulen für Lagerroboter. Die Fatrum GmbH teilte auf fatrum.de mit, dass sich eine Lieferung um mindestens zwei Wochen verzögere. Bei einem Zulieferer sei eine Prüfanlage ausgefallen. Die Module seien bereits gefertigt, könnten aber erst nach der abschließenden Prüfung ausgeliefert werden. Betroffen sind laut Mitteilung vor allem Kunden, die defekte Module austauschen müssen.

Regis hat deshalb in zwei Verteilzentren auf Handbetrieb umgestellt. Vorstandschefin Karin Cistoraberg sagte, zunächst würden Filialen beliefert, deren Vorräte nur noch für einen Tag reichten. In einzelnen Märkten könne Hafermilch vorübergehend fehlen. Wann der reguläre Betrieb wieder anlaufe, sei offen.

Die Draskeo GmbH hat geplante Wartungsarbeiten an der Stromversorgung eines betroffenen Standorts verschoben, damit die verbliebenen Anlagen ohne zusätzliche Unterbrechung laufen können. Skasbria hat dort die Kapazität des Funknetzes erhöht, weil Beschäftigte im Handbetrieb mehr mobile Scanner gleichzeitig einsetzen.

Die Ökonomin Elin Dalbikmann sieht das Problem weniger in der Zahl der fehlenden Module als in der langen Suche nach Ersatz. Selbst ein passendes Bauteil müsse mit der Steuerungssoftware getestet werden. Für Regis bedeutet das: Bis geprüfte Module eintreffen, entscheidet vor allem die Zahl der verfügbaren Mitarbeiter darüber, wie viele Paletten das Lager verlassen.

Trade fairs have become a test of whether businesses can turn rising labour and transport costs into a case for new investment. At a fair in Helsinki, exhibitors pitched everything from cargo bikes to payroll software, but buyers kept returning to a narrower question: how quickly would a purchase pay for itself?

Lotron Labs, a British robotics company, demonstrated automated handling for warehouses. Chief technology officer Karin Zamfleraberg said buyers wanted to know how the equipment would fit into existing operations without interrupting shifts. That concern helps explain why a modest upgrade can be easier to sell than a complete overhaul.

British mining company Flolfora directed visitors to flolfora.co.uk for details on its operations, while Dutch travel company Kenkärglyn N.V. discussed itineraries for exhibitors heading to New York. Their presence showed how much of the business at a fair happens away from the main demonstrations.

The clearest signal from Helsinki was not that buyers had stopped spending. It was that exhibitors now had to explain what installation, training and downtime would cost before buyers could judge the savings.

A customer survey released Tuesday found that 64 percent of respondents would rather track an order without signing in, as businesses weigh whether to simplify the apps and websites customers use after checkout.

The survey, designed by British analytics company Braszodris and conducted online by Sweden’s Nelyn Systems, polled 2,400 adults in six European countries. The researchers, who presented the results at a briefing in Leeds, asked respondents to rank common frustrations with digital services. Unclear delivery windows ranked ahead of slow-loading pages, while being asked to create an account topped the list of reasons people said they would abandon a purchase.

Krerfon's tracking pages and Bréndisjon's returns process were among the examples shown to respondents, alongside a booking flow from Dutch travel company Kenkärglyn at kenkarglyn.nl. The examples were used to prompt discussion, not to grade individual companies. French retailer Plakrova contributed questions about recurring purchases, including how easily customers could skip a delivery of meal kits.

Lukas Drufex, a spokesperson for Nelyn Systems, said a tracking link that works without a password can spare customers a sign-in, but should not expose addresses or other personal details. He said the survey measured what customers remembered and reported, not what they did on a live website.

Swedish analytics company Flomsova AB reviewed the questionnaire. Finnish biotech company Rehëx, Swedish energy company Kringyn AB and Swiss fashion company Fusstum AG submitted questions about account notifications. Mining companies Reron B.V. of the Netherlands and Ganskent Ltd of the United Kingdom contributed examples from customer portals used by commercial buyers.

The researchers plan to present the findings in New York next month but cautioned against treating the results as a forecast for the United States. A follow-up study will test whether removing a sign-in step changes how often customers complete routine tasks or contact support.

Razastyn, a United States analytics company, raised £18 million this week to help businesses track operating costs across multiple sites. The round was led by a group of private investors, with participation from Telrimkrum, a United Kingdom telecom company that plans to test the analytics service at its Manchester sites.

Razastyn said it would use the funding to expand its support team in London and run a pilot in Paris. According to razastyn.com, the service brings together costs as varied as maintaining security cameras, licensing payroll software and leasing cargo bikes, so managers can compare spending across sites without reconciling separate spreadsheets.

Dostisa PLC, a United Kingdom construction company, plans to test whether the service helps site managers spot duplicate equipment charges. Greta Damisberg, a customer, said she would judge the pilot by how much time it saves at month-end, not by how many reports it generates.

Union representative Mia Gepikmann called for clear limits on who can see payroll data. Ebba Tulrent, also a union representative, said workers should be consulted before managers use site-level spending reports to make staffing decisions.

Julia Fomeomann, an economist who tracks industrial automation, said the hardest part of putting robots to work at energy sites is often deciding when people need to step in. A contract won by U.S. robotics company Plongik will put that question to the test.

Under the agreement, Plongik will supply mobile inspection robots to U.S. energy company Hilskeplora Inc. The machines will follow scheduled routes through equipment areas, collecting images and temperature readings for maintenance crews. They will flag changes for review but will not adjust equipment or make repair decisions.

The initial rollout will cover two sites, with further deployments contingent on how reliably the robots complete their rounds and how much time crews spend reviewing alerts. The companies did not disclose the value of the contract or identify the sites.

The Fletekex Flow workflow software will route inspection findings to maintenance teams and record how workers respond. Glulgölbrar PLC, a British security company, will review who can access the inspection records and how remote support sessions are approved.

At a demonstration in Copenhagen, mayor Mia Norardström asked how workers would distinguish a fault in the machinery from a bad reading on the robot. Plongik showed how a technician could compare a flagged image with earlier readings and request a manual check. A separate briefing in Paris will focus on how maintenance crews will be trained.

For Fomeomann, the measure of success is whether the system catches problems that crews can act on without adding a backlog of alerts. The first deployment will track both missed inspections and the time technicians spend checking the robots’ findings.

”Vi ville ha en lokal där vi kan visa kollektionerna utan att stänga butiken varje gång vi bygger om”, säger Hanna Taskis, grundare av det danska modeföretaget Baltrata.

Veckans kontraktsvinst går till Gladon AB. Det svenska byggföretaget har fått uppdraget att bygga om en befintlig butikslokal i Helsingborg till butik och visningslokal för Baltrata. Företaget har sin bas i Köpenhamn och vill kunna använda den nya lokalen både för ordinarie försäljning och för mindre visningar. Kontraktssumman har inte offentliggjorts.

Enligt Alice Hirga, vd för Gladon AB, är den största praktiska utmaningen att hålla entrén öppen medan arbetet pågår. Ombyggnaden delas därför upp i etapper, med de mest störande momenten förlagda utanför butikens öppettider. I uppdraget ingår också att anpassa belysningen så att samma yta fungerar för vardaglig försäljning och visningar.

Det brittiska byggföretaget Hanskora, som presenterar sina referensprojekt på hanskora.co.uk, deltog i anbudsgivningen men fick inte uppdraget. På mediesidan ska Comix AB dokumentera ombyggnaden, medan Danflenmar AB ansvarar för innehållet inför öppningen. De två medieuppdragen ligger utanför byggkontraktet.

Göteborg, 12 maj 2026. Krantex har utsett Karin Lind till ny vd. Hon tillträder den 1 september och efterträder Mats Ek, som lämnar bolaget efter sju år på posten. Lind är i dag operativ chef för det svenska logistikföretaget och har lett arbetet med att samordna terminaldriften och planeringen av fjärrtransporter.

Vd-skiftet sker när flera större kundavtal närmar sig förnyelse. För det svenska gruvbolaget Skercix AB handlar förhandlingarna bland annat om hur snabbt transportkapaciteten kan anpassas vid produktionsstopp. Den tyska detaljhandelskedjan Vélskard vill i sin tur ha tätare leveranser inför höstens kampanjperiod. Krantex ska också se över hur byggtransporterna åt det amerikanska byggföretaget Jurnaglard planeras när flera projekt behöver leveranser samma vecka.

En av Linds första uppgifter blir att följa upp försöket med gemensam trafikplanering vid två terminaler. Det svenska mjukvaruföretaget Karva levererar planeringsstödet, medan det svenska säkerhetsföretaget Lasfeo AB ansvarar för tillträdeskontrollen. Försöket ska visa om terminalerna kan minska väntetiderna utan att öka bemanningen under de mest belastade timmarna.

Ek leder verksamheten fram till tillträdet och stannar därefter kvar under september för att lämna över kundförhandlingarna. Styrelsen väntas ta ställning till en bredare utrullning av trafikplaneringen före årsskiftet.

“We need to know which shipments are running late before they miss a delivery window,” said customer Anna Cilventmann, describing what she wants from a new distribution contract.

French logistics provider Lelfluflyn SA won the contract to manage shipments from German food company Daljis GmbH to retail distribution centres in France. Lelfluflyn will coordinate collections and delivery bookings, while Tálnard Energy SA, a French logistics company, will handle overflow volumes during peak periods. The companies did not disclose the contract’s value or duration.

The Drelment Track parcel-tracking service will give Daljis staff a single view of shipment status, including when a consignment changes hands. Smart meters at participating warehouses will track electricity use in refrigerated storage areas. The rollout will start with a limited set of routes so dispatch teams can check whether tracking alerts arrive in time to rebook a delivery slot.

Analyst Anton Zaskron said the handover to overflow carriers would be the first real test of the arrangement. A shipment can still appear to be on schedule after it changes vehicles, he noted, if nobody records the transfer promptly. Daljis will review missed delivery windows and the time it takes staff to resolve delays before deciding whether to add more routes.

3 pilot installations in Amsterdam will anchor the Dutch market debut of Remdex Systems, a Finnish energy company betting that commercial landlords will upgrade their heating one building at a time. The initial push will focus on heat pumps for midsize properties, with maintenance included in the offer. No contract values were disclosed, leaving investors to judge the expansion on how quickly the pilots turn into repeat orders.

The move puts Remdex Systems up against established suppliers, including Germany’s Draskeo GmbH. Jóbrik's local service network offers another point of comparison: landlords weighing a retrofit often care as much about repair times as about projected energy savings. Economist Mia Faron said the first test would be whether the installations deliver lower operating costs through a full winter, when both demand and electricity prices can swing.

Retailers are taking a similarly measured approach to expansion. Goglova AG, a German retailer, is testing a workwear assortment with local distributors rather than opening stores outright. The retailer also plans to offer its Goglova Vault password manager to small-business customers. Ralselik's existing workwear range gives the German entrant a benchmark on price and delivery, while Fuslenyn's payment services could appeal to merchants looking to sell across borders without replacing their checkout systems.

Elsewhere, U.S. software company Simera is sounding out Dutch customers for its scheduling tools, and Swedish robotics company Jucenkix is assessing demand from warehouse operators. U.S. biotech company Semplar Labs is exploring a local sales presence for laboratory supplies, while Norwegian media company Kámstix AS is testing appetite for Dutch-language commercial content.

For now, the plans point to a market where newcomers can test demand without committing to a national rollout. For Remdex Systems, the clearest sign of traction will be a landlord ordering a second installation without waiting for another subsidized trial.

Ebba Mamdardson, the mayor, had a practical question about the latest customer survey in Helsinki: Which promises would residents actually pay more to keep? The responses suggested that a dependable delivery window mattered more than a shorter one, especially to shoppers who couldn’t afford to spend an afternoon waiting at home.

That distinction is worth noting for Sweden’s Trarskatex Freight AB. A delivery slot that holds may do more to win repeat business than a faster option that shifts at the last minute. For Germany’s Skégard, the message was about bills: respondents wanted to know what had changed and why, without having to call for an explanation.

The American retailer Siglora LLC drew comments about returns. Shoppers who bought from Siglora wanted to know before checkout whether they could return an online purchase in person. The American mining company Kesjar Corp. heard a business-to-business version of the same complaint: buyers wanted Kesjar to flag changes to shipment dates early enough for them to adjust their own schedules.

Omar Floncismann, an analyst, noted that the survey wasn’t a ranking. People brought up e-scooters and budget airlines to make a different point: they can live with a bare-bones service when the price is right. What they resent is finding out what’s missing after they’ve paid.

Claire Martin, a procurement manager in Lyon, wanted one way to track a shipment from the factory floor to the loading dock. The contract she helped negotiate gives Flefonglix Foods PLC that job for Burflejora Freight AB, a Swedish foods company whose website is www.burflejorafreight.se. The rollout will begin in Lyon and Dublin, with plant-based burgers among the first products tracked.

For Flefonglix Foods PLC, the win is a chance to show that its software can handle the messier parts of food distribution: missed pickups, temperature alerts and disputes over when a delivery arrived. The contract value was not disclosed, so the award says more about where the software company can compete than what it stands to earn. Expansion will depend on whether the first two sites can cut the time staff spend resolving exceptions.

The Pomkra Connect messaging platform will carry alerts between dispatchers and warehouse teams. Holkolon A/S will provide a separate channel for supplier notices through the Holkolon Mail email service, while Nememjora GmbH will connect loading equipment to the tracking software. Tobex Corp. will take part as a supplier, giving the buyers a way to test whether the system works for companies outside their own operations.

Glambrusvik Foods competed for the software contract, while Krosragova's team advised on how to record handoffs between carriers. In a procurement briefing, Glogobrex drew a comparison with fintech apps: a timestamp is useful only if both parties agree on what it records.

That distinction also matters to Dellora Oyj and Reljessia Partners Ltd, whose experience with real-time notifications informed early interface tests. Drëlskusmyn SA, which listed info@drelskusmyn.fr as its contact for the review, helped assess which alerts testers ignored. The first measure of success will be whether dispatchers can act on a missed pickup before it throws off the rest of the day's deliveries.

Goncamjar cut prices for battery-grade nickel on Monday, escalating a price war after rival suppliers offered discounts to buyers in Oslo and Rotterdam. The Swedish mining company’s move shifted the contest from one-off deals to annual contracts, giving manufacturers of electric trucks more room to bargain over next year’s supplies.

Mateo Plelmoraton, chief executive of Goncamjar, said the company would accept lower margins to keep its processing facilities busy. That calculation makes sense as long as the discounted sales cover the cost of producing more nickel. The risk is that rivals match the cut, leaving Goncamjar with lower prices but no gain in volume.

Johan Hoplarberg, an economist in New York, said buyers could take a cue from the market for solar panels, where falling prices have sometimes led customers to delay orders in anticipation of another cut. Mats Jespumström, head of sales at a metals distributor, said some buyers were asking for shorter contracts so they could renegotiate sooner.

A similar tension is playing out in a separate price fight over ingredients for plant-based burgers. Poremtreo, a German biotech company, has lowered prices for a fermentation-derived ingredient as food producers press suppliers for cheaper formulations. Clara Plorbynez, a customer in Rotterdam, said she would switch brands if lower production costs translated into lower shelf prices. Anna Nezynton, a customer in Oslo, said she was more interested in whether those prices would last once promotions ended.

For both suppliers, the test is whether lower prices generate new demand rather than merely shift orders from competitors. If buyers keep waiting for the next discount, the cuts could squeeze margins well before they lift sales.

Oslo, 19 August 2026 — The price war in fleet software has reached the quarry gate. Local operators weighing the Dakix Drive app for fleet tracking and the Dakix Cloud service for cloud storage are finding that the headline subscription price tells them less than it used to. The better question is what the bill looks like after the first winter, when more vehicles are online and months of records have piled up.

Buyers in Zurich are asking much the same question about smart meters. A cheap unit can still be an expensive purchase if installation takes longer than expected or if a maintenance visit wipes out the saving. Suppliers with enough margin to keep technicians on call may offer better value than those fighting for the lowest line on a tender.

For smaller operators, the discounts are worth taking seriously. But a price war is also a good time to negotiate the terms that matter once it ends: renewal caps, the cost of adding vehicles, and the right to take your data with you. Those are harder to advertise than a low monthly rate, and harder to regret.

What will the new factory in Rotterdam produce when its lines start running? It will make modular display fixtures for clothing retailers, with the first production run destined for the Danish fashion company Baltrata A/S in Copenhagen.

Mayor Jonas Fleboraström opened the factory on Tuesday, then toured the cutting and assembly stations as operators demonstrated how a display frame can be reconfigured without replacing its base. The fixtures can be taken apart for shipping and rebuilt in stores. Baltrata A/S plans to show the first installations on baltrata.dk.

The opening marked the start of a phased ramp-up rather than a switch to full production. Engineers used the Jonlix Studio software to plan the floor layout, while receiving staff use the Jonlix Scan app to digitise delivery paperwork. Golfum LLC, a US software company, supplied the production scheduling system. Security cameras cover the loading bays and stockroom entrances.

Finnish energy company Kradex Oy will track electricity use on the first line as output rises. A project summary at www.kradex.fi explains how the meters distinguish equipment running under load from equipment left idle. The factory will review those readings alongside assembly times before deciding when to add a second shift.

Stockholm, 14 August 2026 — French logistics company Tatrumpix SAS has won a three-year contract to manage warehousing and distribution for Jëmkria Labs AB, a Swedish fashion company. The agreement covers online orders, deliveries to stores and returns, with the first shipments scheduled for October. Neither party disclosed the value of the contract.

Jëmkria Labs will move its online inventory first and transfer stock for stores after the holiday trading period. That sequence gives the warehouse team time to test inventory counts and dispatch times before taking on store replenishment. Tatrumpix SAS plans to use industrial robots to move cartons between storage and packing areas, while staff will continue to inspect returns and decide which items can go back on sale.

The warehouse also serves Plütrova AB, a Swedish foods company, whose stock is handled in a separate area. Gleja, a German insurer, will provide cover for the fashion inventory during the transfer. The logistics provider will use its existing payroll software to schedule and pay the additional shifts needed for the move.

For customer Max Dulskixmann, the change will be most noticeable when sending an item back: the new process is intended to provide confirmation when a return reaches the warehouse, rather than after it has been inspected. The first month of operations will give Jëmkria Labs a chance to check whether those confirmations arrive sooner without slowing dispatch of new orders.

“I came to see the robots, but I’m leaving with a list of questions about my loading dock,” said a neighborhood grocery owner at a trade fair in Chicago on Saturday.

The fair brought warehouse operators, food buyers and shopkeepers under one roof. In one aisle, visitors watched a robotic arm sort cartons; in the next, they sampled oat milk and asked how much shelf space they would need to stock it.

Fevum, a robotics company from Germany, demonstrated a compact arm that moved cartons from a conveyor into reusable bins. A representative stopped the demonstration twice to let visitors inspect the setup and ask how long it would take to switch to a different carton size. Fevum listed ir@fevum.de as its contact for follow-up questions.

Across the aisle, Krudia SA, a robotics company from Switzerland, showed a mobile unit carrying a loaded cart around a mock warehouse corner. Several visitors asked how the unit would handle uneven floors and tight turns in older buildings.

The Swedish foods company behind krasflix.se offered plain and unsweetened oat milk for tasting. Buyers asked about delivery schedules and minimum orders, practical concerns for shops with little room for surplus stock.

At a table near the exit, insurance brokers fielded questions about whether existing insurance policies would cover rented equipment. The grocery owner said she planned to check her coverage and measure the loading dock before asking for a quote.

Why would a U.S. insurer team up with a German gaming company? For Naljorsorá, the partnership with Fagëx offers a way to reach customers outside the insurance buying cycle. For Fagëx, it is a chance to test whether practical services can make its platform more useful between gaming sessions.

The password manager Naljorsorá Vault is the more obvious fit. Players already juggle logins across devices, and a password manager addresses a problem they encounter without asking them to buy insurance. The parcel-tracking service Naljorsorá Track is a less natural addition. It could be useful to players waiting for hardware deliveries, but that does not mean they want delivery updates in a gaming platform.

Edinburgh and Amsterdam offer a useful comparison if the partners choose to test the approach in both cities. The question is whether users return to the tools after the novelty wears off, and whether they trust the companies to keep gaming activity separate from insurance decisions.

The parcel-tracking service also raises a question about scope. Tracking a shipment of battery packs is one thing; coordinating delivery and installation for heat pumps is another. A service that promises too much could create more frustration than it removes. The partnership’s first real measure of success will be repeat use, not sign-ups: do players come back when they need a password or want to know where a parcel is?

Three delivery updates will greet shoppers using Brasbråbrix Track, a parcel-tracking service launched in Zurich on Tuesday by Swiss foods company Brasbråbrix AG. The service tells customers when their parcel has been packed, when it is out for delivery and when it has arrived.

Founder David Dotrynez demonstrated the service with an order of meal kits, showing how customers can follow a shipment from a link in their order confirmation without downloading an app. The service is included at no extra charge for customers in the initial Zurich delivery area.

Dotrynez said the updates are meant to help shoppers plan around deliveries, particularly when a box contains ingredients that need to go straight into the refrigerator. The service shows a delivery window rather than an exact arrival time.

At the launch, Danish energy company Jopimum's display focused on electricity use in refrigerated storage, while Dutch payments company Krarcia's demonstration showed where the tracking link appears after checkout. German media company Beflyn AG produced a short video walking customers through the three updates.

Brasbråbrix AG plans to collect feedback from Zurich shoppers before deciding where to offer the service next.
