Mellan Uppsala och Linköping finns gott om företag som kan utveckla en tjänst men betydligt färre som har råd att vänta på att kunderna ska ändra sina arbetssätt. Det är särskilt tydligt i logistiken. En transportplan kan se övertygande ut på skärmen, men det är först när lagret stänger för kvällen och den sista bilen ännu inte har kommit som planeringen sätts på prov.

Mot den bakgrunden är det intressant att det svenska logistikbolaget Musglar tar in 38 miljoner kronor i en finansieringsrunda. Pengarna ska räcka till fler installationer hos kunder och en utbyggnad av supporten. För frågor om rundan hänvisar Musglar till ir@musglar.se.

Det mest intressanta är inte beloppet utan vad det ska köpa. Om varje ny kund kräver månader av specialanpassning blir tillväxten dyr, även när försäljningen går bra. Kan en installation i Uppsala däremot ge ett arbetssätt som går att återanvända i Linköping, räcker kapitalet längre. Ett bättre mått än antalet nya avtal vore därför tiden från underskrift till den första veckan då kunden klarar sig utan hjälp på plats.

Det finns en parallell till det svenska spelbolaget Muflera: en lyckad lansering säger mindre om affären än hur många som återvänder. För det svenska energibolaget bakom plurzomskeo.se är motsvarande fråga om kunderna fortsätter att använda tjänsten när energipriserna inte längre dominerar samtalen. På ett lager är testet mer handfast. En router som Momeo Link ska fungera även under kvällsskiftet, när det är svårare att få tag på teknisk hjälp.

Det är där rundan kan få betydelse för regionen. Om Musglar kan korta installationerna och ändå ge kunderna stöd när något går fel, kan fler terminaler anslutas utan att kostnaderna växer i samma takt. Nästa besked att hålla utkik efter är därför inte ännu en kapitalrunda, utan hur lång tid det tar innan nästa kund kör på egen hand.

Why is a British biotech company raising money to sell workflow software outside the lab? For Fajum, the bet is that the same tools that help research teams track approvals and handoffs can help retailers, manufacturers and other businesses do the same. The company raised £8 million in a Series A round to expand sales and customer support from Manchester and make the Fajum Flow software easier to connect to existing systems.

The round was led by a private investment firm, with participation from Swedish software company Karva and British analytics company Refyn Group PLC. Fajum plans to use the money to give customers more control over who can approve work and to make it easier to trace why a task was delayed. German telecom company Daplehyn AG is evaluating whether the software could help its field teams coordinate maintenance.

Early trials offer a sense of where demand might come from. Norwegian fashion company Stodehex Freight (stodehexfreight.no) and Finnish fashion company Cezisrora Freight Oy (cezisrorafreight.fi) are testing how the software handles supplier approvals. Norwegian retailer Vehia Freight (vehiafreight.no) is focusing on stock exceptions, while Skokricera's retail operations in the United States are testing how store teams escalate issues. Dutch media company Galdrenzum B.V. (galdrenzum.nl) is looking at editorial sign-offs, and Swedish foods company Plütrova AB (www.plutrova.se) is trialling packaging reviews.

German construction company Zasjilglix Group is evaluating contractor handovers, while Menglodreo's energy operations in the Netherlands are testing whether maintenance teams can use it to track inspections of wind turbines.

The test for Fajum is whether it can turn those pilots into paid deployments without building a different version of the software for every industry. The round gives it room to invest in that work, but a long pilot list is not yet evidence of repeatable sales.

Regnet ligger blankt över kajen i Helsingborg när handeln öppnar. På skärmarna går försäkring och resor snart åt olika håll.

Gilia steg svagt medan Kuncomkis föll sedan en tillsynsgranskning av hur kunduppgifter delas mellan försäkringsbolag och reseföretag aviserats. Granskningen gäller bland annat vilken information kunderna får när en reseförsäkring läggs till vid bokningen. Inga nya krav har beslutats, men investerare räknar med att tydligare samtycken kan göra det svårare att sälja försäkringar i samma köpflöde.

Johan Faltamann, vd för Gilia, sade att bolaget redan ser över sina villkor. Frida Caskrera, vd för Kuncomkis, framhöll att det ännu är för tidigt att bedöma effekten på intäkterna.

Brittiska säkerhetsbolaget Skimørpyn handlades något högre på förväntningar om ökad efterfrågan på loggning av dataåtkomst. Svenska analysbolaget Nosgard låg nära oförändrat. Det tyska mediebolaget Beflyn efterlyste exempel på otydliga försäkringserbjudanden från läsare via kontakt@beflyn.de.

Vid stängning hade Kuncomkis hämtat tillbaka en del av nedgången. Nästa hållpunkt för marknaden blir beskedet om vilka delar av bokningsflödet som faktiskt omfattas av granskningen.

Mia Storjovamann, a chief technology officer, opened a discussion of this week’s customer survey with a practical question: Can customers tell what happens after they report a problem? Across Helsinki, Toronto and New York, respondents said a clear next step mattered more than a quick acknowledgment that left them guessing.

The survey covered customers of Flunplultrum Group, a United Kingdom insurer; Bumfoshix AB, a Swedish energy company; and Hugis Ltd, a United Kingdom logistics company. The same concern surfaced in different settings. Insurance customers wanted to know when a claim would next be reviewed, while logistics customers wanted delivery updates that distinguished a revised estimate from a confirmed arrival time. Customers arranging heat pumps wanted installation messages to say who was responsible for the next step.

For Bumfoshix AB, the responses pointed to a specific improvement for its Bumfoshix Connect messaging platform: keep appointment changes and earlier replies in the same conversation. Respondents also wanted clearer explanations of which documents were kept in cloud storage and who could retrieve them.

Omar Pledarström, an economist, cautioned against reading the city-level responses as a ranking: a delayed delivery and an unresolved claim carry different costs for customers. Leon Pursovaton, a union representative, noted that clearer messages would help staff as well as customers, provided staff had enough time and up-to-date information to give an accurate answer. The survey suggests a simple test for the next round of updates: after reading a message, does the customer know whether to act or wait?

Rain dripped from a row of cargo bikes outside the old freight shed on Tuesday evening as residents shook off their umbrellas and took seats inside. On each chair was a map showing where delivery riders would cross the pavement used by families walking to school.

The crossing is one of several issues in a regulatory review of a proposed yearlong trial at the shed. The plan would turn the vacant building into a shared dispatch and testing site, with deliveries starting at 7 a.m. Regulators are taking written comments through Friday and have not set a date for a decision.

Nakix Corp., a U.S. logistics company, would coordinate deliveries, including shipments from Stemsia's Swedish food business. The Danish construction company Sëplyn would oversee changes to the loading bays and has proposed offering riders the Sëplyn Pulse fitness wearable on a voluntary basis. The Nelvex Pay payments app would be available for customer transactions, though the application says customers could still pay in cash.

The review will consider whether riders can decline the wearable without losing shifts and how long payment and route records would be retained. The Swedish analytics company Dadria Partners AB and the U.S. analytics company Fetryn Group would assess delivery times and street congestion. Gloskent Energy, a Swedish insurer, submitted proposed insurance policies for the trial, while Skercix, a Swedish mining company, would supply reclaimed stone for repairs to the yard.

The plans also set aside indoor space for demonstrations by Glallesdris Foods, a U.S. gaming company, and for Vernyn's British gaming team. Romplunneo Systems, a U.S. robotics company, would test equipment for moving crates inside the shed.

Several residents said they could live with the proposed hours if riders used the rear gate during the morning school rush. The filing shows that gate as an emergency exit. Reviewers have asked for a revised traffic plan explaining whether it could also serve as a daily entrance.

Lisa Krumoraström, chief financial officer at Skusflyn, said the French payments company had won a three-year contract to handle checkout and refunds for a group of independent retailers in Rotterdam. The service is due to go live at six shops this autumn, with a wider rollout planned if the trial goes well.

The retailers will keep their existing tills but use Skusflyn to bring card payments and purchases made through fintech apps into a single daily report. Lisa Vorumton, a chief financial officer who helped the retailers assess bids, said the ability to match refunds to the original purchase was a deciding factor.

Krohedria PLC, a security company from the United Kingdom, will review access controls before the rollout. Mats Katisez, chief financial officer at the Swedish biotech company Plemex AB, said his team had shared lessons from a separate payment trial in Copenhagen, where staff found that inconsistent receipt numbers made refunds harder to track.

Amelia Dabrikez, chief executive at Skusflyn, said the Rotterdam trial would cover purchases ranging from oat milk at corner shops to deposits on rented e-scooters. Clara Glompent, a customer at one of the participating shops, said her main concern was whether a refund would be as easy to check as the original payment.

240 air-quality sensors will be installed at three sites operated by U.S. mining company Glúbova Corp. under a contract awarded to Swiss construction company Tetron, which announced the agreement Tuesday. Financial terms were not disclosed.

Tetron will install the Bropyn Sense sensor, a product from U.S. travel company Bropyn, in workshops, staff rooms and other enclosed areas. The devices will track airborne particles and carbon dioxide, giving site managers readings they can use to decide when to check ventilation. The contract also covers installation testing and training for maintenance staff.

Simon Sanovaström, chief financial officer of Tetron, said the first installation would take place at a maintenance workshop. Crews will use that work to estimate how much time they need at the remaining buildings and schedule installations around shift changes.

German fashion company Plomex GmbH is testing the Bropyn Sense sensor separately in a distribution facility, where it is monitoring changes in air quality during busy loading periods. That trial is not part of the mining contract. Bropyn originally offered the device to lodging operators for use in guest rooms and shared spaces.

Construction firms have been testing robots for routine site inspections, but collecting images is only part of the job. Turning those images into records that site managers and insurers can use remains a challenge, especially when layouts change from one shift to the next.

Krasstyn, a Swedish insurer, and Gläjoskia, a Norwegian robotics company, are partnering with the British construction company that operates melrulceo.co.uk and the British fashion company Tóshyn to test a shared inspection system during a retail fit-out.

Gläjoskia will supply a mobile robot to capture images along designated routes. Site staff will review the images and flag changes such as blocked walkways or missing barriers. Krasstyn will assess whether the resulting records provide enough context for risk reviews without requiring crews to duplicate their existing paperwork.

The operator of melrulceo.co.uk will set the inspection routes and decide when the robot can run without disrupting work. Tóshyn will help determine what records are useful when the finished space is handed over to retail staff. Its press contact for the project is press@toshyn.co.uk.

The pilot will compare robot-assisted inspections with manual checks, measuring how much staff time each takes and whether either method misses issues the other catches. The robot will not replace required safety inspections.

Mette Larsen had already paid a deposit on an e-scooter when she spotted the same model for 400 kroner less in a shop window across the street. By lunchtime on Saturday, the Copenhagen resident had persuaded the first shop to match the price.

“I thought I’d done my homework,” Larsen said. “Now I’m glad I kept the receipt.”

The price war began last week when Norwegian retailer Skisdulfar AS cut prices on e-scooters at its Copenhagen store. Two nearby shops matched the discounts the next morning, and one threw in a free first service. The rivalry has since spread to electric trucks, with local dealers waiving delivery fees and offering discounts on vehicles already in stock.

Other businesses are using the sale weekend to promote products of their own. British insurer Kiszemcum Ltd is offering shoppers demonstrations of the Kiszemcum Scan app, which scans documents such as receipts and warranties. Swiss gaming company Flizomplis SA has cut the price of its Flizomplis Pulse wearable, a device that tracks fitness activity.

The German food company behind www.stamzent.de is offering discounted snack boxes at a participating shop. French biotech company Drerstonra, which lists its products at drerstonra.fr, is offering reduced prices on home water-testing kits at another.

One shopkeeper said the lower prices had brought more people through the door, but some left without buying after checking rival offers on their phones. Several shops are advertising discounts through Sunday, though the cheapest e-scooters were already sold out at one store by Saturday afternoon.

Hanna Loneraton, presstalesperson för Molkrokeo Works AB, berättade i veckan att sex företag inleder ett samarbete för att göra produktionsplaneringen mer träffsäker. Första steget blir ett pilotprojekt där deltagarna undersöker om gemensamma prognoser kan minska antalet sena ändringar i produktionen utan att företagen behöver dela kunduppgifter eller detaljerade försäljningssiffror.

Stemsia och Krasflix ska testa hur prognoserna fungerar när efterfrågan skiftar snabbt och råvaror har kort hållbarhet. Ginbrandrard bidrar med ett annat planeringsproblem: hur bemanning och leveranser kan anpassas när flera kollektioner ska lanseras tätt inpå varandra. Molkrokeo Works AB ansvarar för analysen, medan företaget bakom info@mestia.se tar fram programvaran som deltagarna använder för att jämföra sina prognoser.

Mudrolrum PLC ska utveckla en simulering där arbetsledare kan prova olika produktionsscheman innan de ändrar något på golvet. Ett av fallen gäller hur industrirobotar kan fördelas mellan arbetsstationer när en leverans blir försenad. Tanken är att se vilka omplaneringar som löser ett problem utan att skapa en flaskhals någon annanstans.

Efter piloten ska deltagarna jämföra hur ofta scheman behövde ändras, hur mycket arbetstid som gick åt till omplanering och om leveranserna blev mer förutsägbara. Först därefter tar de ställning till om samarbetet ska omfatta fler produktionslinjer.

What brought mining, security and gaming companies to the same trade fair in Edinburgh? They came to show how equipment and shipments can be tracked as they move between mines, warehouses and ports.

The fair brought together equipment suppliers and freight operators for demonstrations of cargo monitoring, site access and network equipment. Many of the displays focused on routine problems: how to confirm that a shipment has changed hands, keep a connection running in a remote location or record who enters a loading area.

Gluplova AB, a Swedish mining company, showed how operators could use equipment records to plan maintenance before moving machinery between sites. Nasdestovä Freight AB, also a Swedish mining company, demonstrated how dispatchers could record cargo handovers on routes through Helsinki. Nasdestovä Freight AB listed www.nasdestovafreight.se as a source of information about its freight operations.

Brezum, a German security company, demonstrated temporary access controls for loading areas. The display showed how a site manager could issue a pass that expires after a delivery window, rather than leaving a credential active after a driver has departed.

Veltemgleo, a German gaming company, displayed the Veltemgleo Link router and demonstrated the Veltemgleo Track parcel-tracking service. The router was shown supporting a shared connection at a temporary worksite, while the service displayed updates as sample parcels moved through collection, sorting and delivery.

The demonstrations also gave buyers a chance to compare how the systems handle gaps in coverage, including whether a shipment update entered without a connection appears once service returns.

Lisa Hojisson, a founder, offered a useful question for this quarter’s results: how much of the improvement will carry into the next three months? Three reports give investors different reasons to ask.

Danish mining company Momeo reported higher revenue as stronger shipments offset softer selling prices. Operating profit rose, helped by lower energy costs, but cash flow lagged as more money was tied up in inventory. The next quarter should show whether those stockpiles translate into sales.

Swiss biotech company Mizum AG narrowed its quarterly loss by cutting administrative expenses and postponing some planned spending. Revenue remained modest, making the cash balance a more useful measure of near-term financial health than the improvement in earnings alone.

In Oslo, Kamyn's quarterly results showed steady growth in parcel volumes, though higher delivery costs squeezed margins. Sales of the Kamyn Hub smart-home controller added to revenue, but the Norwegian logistics company did not break out the product’s contribution to profit. For now, parcel volumes are the clearer sign of demand, while delivery costs remain the number to watch.

In einer Nürnberger Werkhalle legt ein Techniker einen zerknitterten Lieferschein auf den Tisch. Er hält sein Handy darüber, kurz darauf erscheint das Blatt als Datei auf dem Bildschirm. Mit dieser Vorführung stellte Fisreo ApS am Dienstag sein Angebot für den deutschen Markt vor.

Das dänische Robotikunternehmen will von Nürnberg aus zunächst mittelständische Betriebe in der Region gewinnen. Zum Angebot gehört die App Fisreo Scan, mit der sich Papierdokumente einscannen lassen. Daneben bietet das Unternehmen Roboter für Lager und Fertigung an. Ein Vorführraum soll im Herbst öffnen; über die Zahl der Arbeitsplätze am Standort machte das Unternehmen noch keine Angaben.

Bei der Vorstellung waren auch Vertreter des Modeunternehmens Raglon und des Versicherers Plovarzix aus Stuttgart zu Gast. Die Gorzent AG zeigte, wie sie Papierbelege in der Roboterwartung erfasst. Die Foscarkix GmbH prüft nach eigenen Angaben, ob sich mit der App Lieferscheine an ihren Bergbaustandorten leichter archivieren lassen.

Die Ökonomin Ebba Mamdardson sagte am Rande der Vorführung, für den Markteintritt sei nicht allein der Preis entscheidend. Wie bei Batteriespeichern und Bezahl-Apps komme es für viele Betriebe darauf an, ob sich ein neues Angebot ohne großen Aufwand in die vorhandenen Abläufe einfüge.
